Neonatal Milk sharks (Rhizoprionodon acutus) emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 34 cm [Lb = approximately 34 cm], a modest size that reflects the energetic constraints of gestation within this viviparous carcharhinid. Field records from the Gulf of Mexico indicate that parturition follows a gestation period of roughly 310 days [ab = roughly 310 days] when ambient water temperatures average 31 °C [T = 31 °C], a thermal regime typical of their subtropical nursery grounds. These shallow coastal nurseries, often enriched with organic detritus, provide abundant small teleost and crustacean prey that supports rapid early growth. The neonatal length at birth of around 34 cm [Lb = around 34 cm] places them among the smaller Carcharhiniformes at parturition, a trait that likely heightens vulnerability to larger piscivorous predators such as bull sharks during the first few months of life. Pups rely initially on internal yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding, a period during which their growth trajectory is strongly influenced by local prey density and thermal conditions.

As the juvenile shark matures, distinct sex-based differences in body size become apparent. The total length at which females attain sexual maturity has been reported at 70 cm [Lp = 70 cm], whereas males reach puberty at a slightly smaller 68 cm [Lp = 68 cm]. This sex-specific divergence in maturation length is a common pattern among carcharhinids and is thought to reflect the greater energetic demands of gestation and parturition in females, which favors a larger body size to accommodate reproductive output. Pop-up archival tag data from the northwestern Atlantic suggest that growth rates slow considerably upon the onset of gonadal maturation, with both sexes investing more heavily in somatic energy reserves as they approach their reproductive length thresholds. The maturational lengths documented for Rhizoprionodon acutus are intermediate among the Rhizoprionodon genus, with R. taylori maturing earlier and at smaller sizes, while R. oligolinx delays maturation to a slightly greater total length.

The ultimate total length attained by adult female Milk sharks has been documented at 133 cm [Li = 133 cm], considerably exceeding the 111 cm [Li = 111 cm] maximum recorded for males, a difference that aligns with the species' pronounced sexual size dimorphism. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size correlates with the large ultimate wet weight of females, which can reach 2750 grams [Wwi = 2750 grams] in mature individuals. The heavier body mass in females accommodates the energetic reserves necessary for supporting developing embryos through a protracted gestation of over ten months (310 days) [ab = 310 days] at 31 °C [T = 31 °C]. Male Milk sharks remain substantially lighter, rarely exceeding 2000 grams in the largest specimens, a pattern consistent with the absence of male parental investment and a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid male maturation and mating frequency over extreme somatic growth. The asymptotic sizes observed in Gulf populations are comparable to those reported from the Arabian Sea, though specimens from cooler Benguela Current waters appear to reach slightly smaller maximum lengths.

Reproductive output in Rhizoprionodon acutus is characterized by a low but consistent fecundity. Gravid females examined from Indian Ocean trawl surveys carry an average of 2 to 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 3 pups per litter], with one litter produced each year [F_R_i = one litter produced each year]. This annual reproductive schedule is closely tied to the species’ seasonal migrations and the thermal windows of their nursery habitats. At a stable water temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], the maximal rate of reproductive output equates to roughly 4.2 pups per 365-day year [Ri = roughly 4.2 pups per 365-day year], a value derived from the interaction of litter size and inter-birth interval. Such a rate is modest when compared to the prolific reproductive output of some hammerhead or requiem sharks, but it aligns well with the life-history strategy of a relatively small coastal carcharhinid. The low fecundity is offset by a moderate birth size that enhances neonatal survival, creating a trade-off between quantity and quality of offspring that is typical of slow-growing elasmobranchs.

The maximum lifespan of the Milk shark has been estimated at approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] based on vertebral banding counts from specimens captured in the Gulf of Mexico at 31 °C [T = 31 °C]. This relatively short longevity for a carcharhinid underscores the species’ position near the fast end of the elasmobranch life-history continuum. By comparison, larger-bodied relatives such as the spinner shark may live two to three times longer.
